1:
The objection is the one the previous two chapters invite, and Gill states it as an adversary would. If the calling of the Gentiles and the setting aside of Israel are what Moses and Isaiah foretold, then where is the covenant with Abraham, what has become of the promises, how is God's faithfulness to be accounted for, and what hope has any Israelite of ever obtaining salvation? Nothing, Gill says, could be thought more injurious to God or more absurd in itself; and he adds that the confidence that God never would nor has cast off that nation was an old prejudice, still held in his own day as an article of the Jewish creed. Barnes frames the same complaint from inside the privileges — the adoption, the promises, the covenant — and puts his finger on the word Paul never said. The objection is built on the supposition that God had rejected all his people, and that supposition is what the chapter dismantles: first by Paul's own case, then by the reserved remnant, then by scripture's warrant for a partial hardening, then by the purpose the rejection served, and last by the return still to come.

How much is being denied turns on the verb. Clarke derives it from the preposition and the verb meaning to thrust or drive, and so reads the question as whether God has thrust Israel off and driven them eternally from him; the rejection Paul repudiates is the universal and the final one, not every kind. Robertson adds that the interrogative particle expects an indignant No, reinforced by the strongest negation Paul owns, and recalls that God had bound himself three times over on this point (1 Samuel 12:22, Psalms 94:14).

Then the apostle produces himself. Barnes takes the argument to be strictly personal: if every son of Abraham must be cut off, Paul must be cut off too, and he plainly is not — so the descent, the tribe, the whole pedigree he was entitled to plead is entered as evidence. Henry hears it as the same argument in the first person, that to say the Jews are all rejected would be to cut off his own claims and see himself abandoned. Ellicott resists the usual reading. The appeal is called out by Paul's sympathy with his countrymen rather than by any anxiety for himself; self-interest sits badly with the generous chivalry of a man who had just wished himself accursed for them (Romans 9:3). On the tribe he is more precise than the others: Benjamin was of the purest blood, since Judah and Benjamin alone kept up the continuity of the race after the Exile. Calvin will not have the tribe made into a display of mercy toward a nearly destroyed clan — that reading he calls forced and far-fetched — and takes the whole recital to establish only that Paul is a native Israelite and no proselyte, so that God's favour resting on him is evidence of favour resting on Israel. Theodoret notices how much Paul passed over: the three thousand of Pentecost, the myriads James spoke of, the believing Jews scattered through the land, any of whom would have served; instead of all these he instances himself.
2:
Paul's denial arrives with a qualification attached, and Calvin makes the structure of it the key to the chapter. An unqualified No would have contradicted everything said in chapters nine and ten; so the answer divides. God has not cast away the race of Abraham contrary to his own covenant, and yet the fruit of adoption does not belong to all the children of the flesh, because a secret election runs beneath the visible people. The visible body was rejected in such a way that no member of the spiritual body of Christ was cut off. To the natural objection — was not circumcision a common badge of favour to every Jew? — he answers that an outward call is ineffectual without faith, and the honour that unbelief refuses is justly withdrawn.

Everything then rests on what the participle means. Barnes denies it is bare foresight: it carries a previous purpose, and the sentence declares a principle of government, that God does not change and will not reject those he had designated as his own. He draws the consequence that the truly renewed persevere. Calvin is blunter. The word is not some foresight by which God observes what a man will turn out to be, but the good pleasure by which he chose as sons those who, being unborn, could procure no favour for themselves; and the proof is downstream, in a remnant reserved according to the election of grace, which cannot be gratuitous if foreseen works decide it. He appeals to Augustine, and to the Galatians who had been known of God in the sense that his favour anticipated them (Galatians 4:9). Gill works the same ground from the other end: all mankind are in a sense God's people, being kept in being by him, but were all foreknown they would all be predestinated, called, justified and glorified, which they are not.

Two of the witnesses pull against this. Ellicott warns that the phrase must not be pressed into an absolute indefectibility of divine favour; God, having set his choice on Israel, will not readily disown them, and their case is not as bad as it looks. Clarke reads the verb as loved or approved, the ordinary force of the Hebrew and Greek words for knowing, and takes the promise to be of special favour rather than of an unbreakable decree. Wesley cuts through by treating the tense as accommodation: knowing and foreknowing are one thing with God, who sees all at once from everlasting to everlasting, and the language speaks after the manner of men. Theodoret glosses the clause as marking those who proved worthy of the divine knowledge by welcoming the light of faith, and hears in it Paul's own security — had God cast them off, he too would have stood condemned, sprung as he is from that root.

The appeal to Elijah is introduced by a formula the commentators pause over. Barnes explains that with no chapters or verses to cite, the Old Testament was quoted by subject, so in Elijah means the passage that tells his story, exactly as at the bush does elsewhere (Luke 20:37). Robertson notes that the verb for pleading is neutral in itself — to fall in with someone, and so to converse, to intercede, or to accuse — and that the hostility is carried entirely by the preposition that follows.
3:
The complaint Paul quotes is Elijah's at Horeb, and Barnes begins by observing that the citation is free: the words are not reproduced exactly, though the sense is kept. The charge itself was true. Prophets had been killed, and Gill traces the order to Jezebel and notes that Christ and the apostles lay the same crime at that nation's door in later generations; he also observes that the Kings text adds with the sword, specifying the manner of death, and that the clause stands elsewhere in the original by a rule of transposition. What Barnes will not grant is the inference. That prophets were murdered proved the character of the nation; it did not prove there were no godly men left in it, and the answer Elijah is about to receive shows the reasoning to have been unfounded.

The demolished altars raise a question of law, and Lightfoot is the one who asks it. What altars of God were there in Samaria for Israelites to throw down? The altar in the temple stood untouched, and by the strict rule there was no other. He answers from a Jewish authority that these were private altars raised to the name of God — one of them the very altar Elijah repaired when he found it broken down (1 Kings 18:30) — and that such high places were lawful enough before the temple was built. Afterwards their use became faulty, since worshippers were bound to the one altar; but Lightfoot draws a distinction the geography forces. For Judah and Benjamin the road to Jerusalem lay open, so private altars there were indefensible; for the ten tribes shut inside the northern kingdom no such access existed, and he leaves it a question whether Elijah would have called the altars of that region unlawful at all.

Barnes supplies the ritual detail behind the verb. The law required altars of earth or unhewn stone (Exodus 20:24), so to dig them down is to level them completely, an act expressive of open impiety; and though one great altar stood before the tabernacle and the temple, others were not forbidden, which is why they appear scattered through the histories. Robertson confirms that the verb for digging under is found nowhere else in the New Testament, that the Greek Old Testament had a milder word, and that Paul has reversed the order of the two clauses he found there, naming the prophets before the altars.

What remains is the loneliness. Ellicott trims the claim to its real extent — left alone, that is, of the prophets — and Clarke reads the whole speech as a man's report that no prophet besides himself survives and that his own life is hunted. Barnes fills in why the prophet could believe it. Obadiah had hidden a hundred in a cave, but the way he speaks of them afterwards suggests they had since been found and killed; the prophets of Baal had just been destroyed, and Ahab and Jezebel wanted the man who destroyed them. Few periods, Barnes says, have gathered so many disheartening things at once: the priesthood of God slaughtered, the nation running to idolatry, the civil power itself leading the apostasy, and every influence of wealth and rank set against the truth. That a solitary man should feel powerless in it he treats as natural rather than culpable. Robertson calls the mood simple dejection, and warns against pressing the word Elijah uses for his threatened life into any technical division of human nature.
4:
What answers the complaint is a word with a formal weight to it. Barnes observes that the noun occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means an oracle, a divine response, without indicating how it came; Robertson notes the same rarity and points to the related verb used of the warnings given to the magi and to Simeon. Gill supplies what the history records — the still small voice — and identifies it with what the rabbis called the daughter of a voice. Such an answer would silence every murmur, and Barnes marks that it came not in the wind or the earthquake but quietly.

The verb of reserving is where the commentators put the weight. Barnes renders the Hebrew as I have caused to remain and insists the honour is claimed by God and traced to nothing in the men; amid a general corruption he had restrained a part. The reservation was to myself, for God's own service and glory. Barnes turns the reservation into a lesson about perception. Elijah supposed he was alone, and at that moment there were thousands; so in the darkest times of the church there may be many more friends of God than anyone supposes, and the number of them is not to be estimated from what a disheartened man can see. Theodoret works the same point into a direct address. All of them were called Israel, and God named himself the God of seven thousand and rejected the rest; and the prophet, one of them, did not know these existed. It is nothing new, he says, if you likewise do not know who among you has fixed his faith in the Saviour, though God acknowledges them as his people. He also presses Elijah's second charge before it is answered: granting that the people were ill-disposed toward prophets who denounced bitter things against them, what quarrel had they with the altars?

The number is read as approximate. Clarke takes seven as a certain figure standing for an uncertain one, and explains the invisibility practically: Jezebel's persecution forced them to conceal their attachment to the true religion, and providence preserved them from her rage. Barnes agrees that seven often marks a round number and turns it into encouragement — in the darkest times there may be far more friends of God than we suppose. He identifies the rival too: the name means lord or master, the deity the Assyrians called Bel, imaged as a bull or a calf.

Two witnesses stop at the grammar of the idol's name. Ellicott notes that the article here is feminine, as often in the Greek Old Testament, and that this is why the translators inserted the word image; how the feminine arose he leaves open, reporting the guesses that the deity was androgynous or that the gender is contemptuous. Robertson gives the explanation Ellicott withholds: the Jews substituted the word for shame when reading the name aloud, and the feminine article followed that noun. Lightfoot uses the verse against those who would correct the Hebrew by the Greek and credit the translators with prophetic inspiration. Paul and they differ twice — thou shalt leave against I have reserved to myself, which he calls no small difference, and again in the article — so one has misremembered, and he asks which. He doubts the arithmetic taken strictly as well: were there only seven thousand in all ten tribes who refused this idol? Perhaps, he says, seventy thousand.
5:
The Elijah episode was cited to license a conclusion about the present, and Gill fixes when the present is: the time of the preaching of the gospel, the accepted time, when the word went to the Gentiles and multitudes of them believed, while the Jews as a body had rejected the Messiah, killed the Lord Jesus, persecuted the apostles and blasphemed the gospel. Even then, he says, God had made a reserve for himself. Barnes runs the parallel out point by point. In Elijah's day everything looked dark and one man alone appeared faithful, yet there was a considerable number of God's true friends; so now, though the nation had rejected its Messiah and would as a consequence be set aside as a nation, it did not follow that anyone was excluded whom God had purposed to save. He is careful not to name a figure, but holds that a multitude of Jews had in fact become Christians — a remnant only when set beside the multitude who refused.

Barnes then turns the history into four things to learn from. That love waxing cold and iniquity abounding is no unparalleled thing. That the right response is deep feeling, as in the psalmist whose eyes ran down with water because men kept not the law (Psalms 119:136). That such times are no warrant for discouragement, since there may be more piety about than despondency can see. And that if all are not corrupted it is God's doing and not theirs, so that the same mercy which reserved a people then may be trusted to meet abounding evil still.

On the phrase itself the witnesses divide sharply, and the division decides how the rest of the chapter will be read. Robertson notes only that the noun for remnant appears here alone in the New Testament, is found in the papyri, and that the election is wholly God's. Clarke will not let the word carry a decree. The election of grace, on his account, is simply God's gracious design in sending the Christian system into the world and saving under it everyone who believes in Christ and no one else; believers are chosen to inherit the blessings of the gospel, while those seeking justification by works of law are rejected. Wesley compresses the same reading into a sentence — the gracious purpose being that he who believes shall be saved. Gill and Barnes stand on the other side, taking the reservation to be a choosing that precedes and produces the believing.

Lightfoot presses a different question, and dissents from the whole drift the chapter is usually given. Granting that the nation at large had been cast off, he says, there was in every age a remnant according to the election of grace, and more conspicuously in the age when Christ and his gospel began to shine out. What he fastens on is the time-marker. Paul says at this present time, and Lightfoot reads the argument as strictly contemporary: has God cast away his people? No, for I am an Israelite and he has not cast me off; and as there was a remnant in Elijah's day, so there is one now. He asks how anything could be more plainly said, and treats the phrase as evidence against reading the passage as a promise of some future call of the whole nation. The objection is lodged, that is, against the future-restoration reading before the chapter has finished building it.
6:
Having called the remnant a matter of grace, Paul turns on the word and refuses to let anything share it. Gill takes the argument to be about election specifically: no reason can be given why God chose one and not another beyond his own pleasure and that unmerited love with which he loves one and not another, not because they were better or would do better; election passed before any works were done, and works rightly done spring from it, so they can never be its rule or measure or condition. Calvin generalises the same logic. Paul is not speaking here of reconciliation, or of the means or nearer causes of salvation, but has gone higher, to why God before the foundation of the world chose some and passed by others; and if any place is given to works, so much is taken from grace. He names the target — those who make foreseen worthiness the ground of election — and points out that it makes no difference whether the works are past or future, since the statement excludes both. He adds that although the sentence is framed around election, the reasoning is general enough to cover the whole of salvation, so that wherever merit is denied, our salvation is being ascribed to grace.

Barnes turns it into a transaction. If men are justified by works it is not favour but debt, and a debt paid confers no obligation on anyone; grace would have to change its nature to survive the mixture. He states the conclusion the mixture forbids: salvation cannot be partly of grace and partly of works, and a man unwilling to have eternal life on those terms cannot have it at all. Robertson's note is on the tense — grace does not merely cease to be grace but stops becoming it, losing its character. Wesley extends the exclusion to works of every kind, ceremonial and moral alike, and treats the two halves as one impossibility: what is given for work is the payment of a debt, and the same benefit cannot in the nature of things arise from both. Theodoret reads the works negatively as the polity of the law, and observes that this is why salvation is itself called grace, since it proceeds from the divine kindness.

Clarke accepts the antithesis and empties the election of its particularity. What is denied, he says, is that the believing Jews were singled out by a sovereign act which might as easily have taken in the whole nation; what is meant is the general scheme by which God resolved to receive into his kingdom anyone, Jew or Gentile, who believes on Christ. He draws the two consequences that follow from that reading and from no other: these same believers would have been excluded had they remained in unbelief like the rest, and every Jew without exception, sinners though they were, would have been taken into this election had they believed. Set beside Calvin's account of a choice made before the world was founded, the two readings of the one phrase can hardly be brought nearer.

Ellicott and Calvin both raise the text. Ellicott reports that the true text differs considerably from the longer form the Authorised Version renders, and states what survives either way: the preservation of the remnant cannot be owing to grace and works at once, but must be owing to one or the other. Calvin gives the evidence. Griesbach judged the second half spurious, since the bulk of the manuscripts and the Latin fathers lack it, though several Greek fathers have it and the old versions carry the whole verse; the argument is complete without it, being the first half restated. He defends it on style — Paul often puts a thing positively and negatively — and notes that Beza, Pareus and Wolfius held it genuine and that Doddridge and Macknight kept it.
7:
Theodoret asks first where the sentence breaks. The opening two words are a question standing by itself — what shall we say to this? — and everything after is the reply. His answer is that Israel missed the mark by clinging to the law, still observing it now against its own intent and reaping no righteousness from it, while those among them who believed obtained what the rest were after. Chrysostom watches Paul's tact rather than his logic. Having shown that the greater part were lost, and not wishing to seem to bring an accusation of his own or to attack his nation as an enemy would, he takes refuge in David and Isaiah and lets the prophets say it. Chrysostom also hears the clause about those who did obtain as an argument from example, on the pattern of the exorcism saying — if your own children cast out devils, they shall be your judges (Luke 11:19) — so that no one can blame the thing sought instead of his own temper. Naming them the chosen, he adds, shows the grace from above and their own eagerness together, and does not deny free will.

Calvin reads the same clause as excluding it. The question is put as though in doubt so that the answer may land the harder, and no other answer is possible: Israel laboured in vain because the attempt was absurd. What follows he treats as the proof — if Israel gained nothing by merit, what did the others gain, whose case was no better? Where does so much difference between equals come from? He allows that the abstract noun may stand for the elect themselves, provided it is granted that more is said thereby than the elect would say, namely that these are not the men who strove by leaning on merits but the men whose salvation hangs on God's free choosing. And since the elect alone are delivered, all who are not chosen must remain hardened; the beginning of the reprobate's ruin is simply that God forsakes them.

Calvin then raises the difficulty against himself, and it is the sharpest thing in the verse. Examined in their own contexts, the passages he is about to quote all present hardening as a scourge with which God punished crimes already committed — whereas the argument here wants men hardened who were rejected before the world was founded. His way out is that reprobation is the root and the punishing blindness the fruit, so that the proximate causes may be stated without cancelling the hidden one. The editor of his text appends a flat demurrer: the reasoning is not satisfactory and goes beyond the Apostle's evident meaning, since the prophets uniformly state the hardening as punishment for previous impenitence, as Calvin himself admits; what must be left to the will of God is only why some were hardened and others softened, and it is neither wise nor right to go past what is expressly taught.

Barnes keeps to that shorter line without argument. The verse affirms that the rest were hardened and says nothing about how it was done; of the election it is expressly said to be of God, of the remainder only the fact is given. Wesley makes the cause their own wilful prejudice. On the word itself the philologists agree and correct the translators. Ellicott calls blinded an erroneous rendering that arose from confusing two similar words, gives hardened as correct, extends the correction to three other places where the same mistake stands, and notes it was a medical term for the forming of chalkstone. Barnes traces it to the callus that knits a broken bone or stiffens a joint, and thinks it was applied to a growth in the eye as well, which is how the sense of blindness attached; Robertson keeps to the covering of thick skin.
8:
The quotation is composite, and the commentators say so plainly. Barnes takes the principal source to be Isaiah 29:10, with Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 6:9 supplying the clause about eyes and ears, and notes that the words follow neither the Hebrew nor the Greek exactly though the sense is kept; Ellicott calls it a free combination of two passages put together, no doubt, from memory. The prefatory phrase, Barnes adds, means upon the same principle — the fact and the manner alike answering to the old declaration.

Most of the labour goes into one noun. Lightfoot states the problem: the Greek word properly denotes remorse or compunction, which is wide of what both prophet and apostle mean. His explanation is a general charge against the translators, that being Jews they sometimes framed a sense of their own foreign to the Hebrew and used Greek words outside the common idiom; and this word in particular they bent, whether they took it from the verb to prick, or from the verb to grieve, or had an eye to the word for night, until it carried the sense of silence, astonishment and horror. Ellicott tells the story more mildly, as a case of two unconnected roots — one meaning to prick or cut with a sharp instrument, the other drowsiness — and thinks the confusion between them real but the outcome settled: from the notion of a sharp wound came the bewilderment consequent on such a blow, and from that stupor in general. Robertson accepts the finished sense and adds a psychological guess, that the torpor looks like the result of too much sensation, dulled by incitement into apathy. Barnes wants the milder word: the Greek admits compunction, which is why the margin offers remorse, but the meaning here is whatever benumbs the faculties, that is, insensibility. Calvin wants the sharper. He refuses to call it the spirit of giddiness, and insists on compunction — the bitterness of gall showing itself, a fury in rejecting the truth — so that what is described is not torpor but active malice, the reprobate so demented by a secret judgment that they cannot form a judgment at all.

Theodoret denies the agency outright. Gave here means gave up, as earlier in the letter, that is, permitted; God did not incline them to unbelief, for how could he inflict infidelity and then require vengeance for it? He points to the prophet's own fuller wording, where the people's heart waxes gross and their ears are dull and their eyes they have closed. Not another has blinded them, he concludes, but they have closed their own eyes and refused the light; and the spirit of slumber means a fixed and obdurate mind, since a man in sound sleep is open to no change for the worse, as one wholly surrendered to evil admits no change for the better. Clarke holds both ends at once: they wilfully shut their eyes against the light, and God in judgment then gave them up to slumber, so that the very word which should have woken them became a savour of death. Wesley says the Spirit was at length withdrawn.

The closing words are made to do work. Calvin sees Paul forestalling the objection that the prophecy had already been discharged in its own age and could not be pressed into the gospel's; the added clause answers it, extending the blindness and the unhealable obstinacy down to the coming of Christ. Barnes reads the same words as reaching to his own day: what was true of the nation in Isaiah's time was true in Paul's, and their refusal of the gospel developed nothing new in them. Robertson notes that the two clauses about not seeing and not hearing are cast as expressions of purpose.
9:
Who is speaking is disputed before anything else is settled. Gill has Christ speaking by the mouth of David, or David in the person of Christ, since the psalm is a prophecy of the Messiah, quoted as such elsewhere; and on that footing he denies that the words are imprecations at all, calling them predictions of what should befall the nation in recompense for giving the Messiah gall for meat and vinegar to drink. Barnes notes the same setting — the citation follows immediately on the verse about the gall and vinegar — and sets the Hebrew, the Greek and the old Aramaic forms side by side to show that Paul kept the sense and not the letter. Ellicott doubts the ascription. It seems to him highly improbable that the psalm was written by David, and he takes the name to stand for the Book of Psalms, with which it was traditionally connected, so that no argument for authorship can be built here. He also finds one of the four words wanting in both Hebrew and Greek, apparently Paul's own addition, and would render it not trap but chase: instead of feasting, let them be hunted.

The table is read two ways. Barnes takes it for food and for the security that goes with it, so that the petition is that what they looked to for refreshment should be sprung on them like a fowler's snare — a thing that happens, he says, whenever temporal enjoyments crowd God out and leave a man indifferent to his own soul. Theodoret hears in the word their luxurious living, prophesied to be exchanged for its opposite. Calvin reports Grotius taking it for the guests who share what is spread on it, and finds the reading striking, since it was the confederates of the Jews who turned enemies and effected their ruin (Jeremiah 38:22); Pareus, he adds, counted three distinct images in the clause — the ensnaring of birds, the entrapping of beasts, and the stumbling of men in the dark — and made the last term mean that being ensnared was the just return for having ensnared others. Robertson keeps the four nouns separate and technical: bird-snares, the hunting of beasts, the trigger a man trips over, and repayment, the last found nowhere else in a bad sense.

Whether such a prayer may be prayed is the question underneath, and Calvin faces it directly. Cursing is forbidden under law and gospel alike, and Christ prayed for his enemies from the cross; yet God cursed every transgressor, Christ cursed two cities, the Psalmist called down vengeance repeatedly, Paul named Alexander the coppersmith (2 Timothy 4:14), and John forbids praying for the man who sins unto death. His resolution is that circumstances make the difference: the rule is to bless, and to pronounce on God's enemies only the judgment God has already declared, while cursing individuals is permitted to none but those inspired to know who has been finally given up — which he supposes of the Psalmist and of Paul. Barnes declines the question and converts it. He will not say whether the prayer was right or wrong; what matters for the argument is that Paul is treating the words as prediction, and that the prediction had by his own day come true, the nation's very privileges having become the occasion of its blindness. Clarke gets there by another road, reasoning from their present temper that what fell on the disobedient before will fall on them again, their blessings turned to curses and their earthly mercies made their whole recompense; and he puts the cause in a sentence — they would have a worldly Messiah, and so rejected the one whose kingdom was not of this world. Wesley notes that the same imprecation fits Judas, and that here sin is punished by sin.
10:
Gill will not have the darkening taken literally. It is not the blindness the angels struck the men of Sodom with, nor the blindness Paul himself inflicted on the sorcerer, but the understanding darkened — by themselves, by Satan, and judicially by God — so that they could not see how the prophecies of Messiah met in Jesus of Nazareth, and found no beauty in his person, nothing wonderful in his works, nothing amiable in his doctrine. He then presses the point past the spiritual into the civil. Not only were the things of the gospel hid from their doctors and rabbis; the things belonging to their own peace and safety were hid too, and never, he says, did a people act more imprudently for its own temporal welfare.

Ellicott glosses both halves as figures for one condition, spiritual blindness and a back bent under spiritual bondage, and quotes Perowne on the Hebrew idiom: darkened eyes stand for weakness and perplexity, as enlightened eyes stand for recovered vigour, and shaking loins express terror, dismay and feebleness. Barnes gives the Hebrew as let their loins totter, the posture of a man under a weight too heavy for him, and takes the clause to ask that they be put to bearing burdens and oppression as the reward of their sin — which he judges to have visibly happened, and to have happened for the reason the psalm assigns. Robertson keeps the harshness audible, calling it a terrible imprecation, and finds in the second verb the bending of captives whose backs are doubled under a load, with a noun for the back that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Clarke insists the mood is misread: the words are declarative and not imprecatory, God stating what will be the case of such unbelievers rather than asking for it — their blessings turned into a snare, their eyes darkened further as they persist, and their backs bowed in abject subjection until they acknowledge Jesus as the Messiah.

Barnes uses the verse to open a longer question, since the difficulty of reconciling the petitions of the Psalms with the temper of the New Testament will not go away by softening a word. He does not think every such petition can be reconciled, and thinks it not at all improbable that many of them were wrong. His account of inspiration is what carries the weight. David was not a perfect man, and the Spirit of inspiration is not answerable for his imperfections; every doctrine delivered is true and every fact recorded is recorded as it was, but it does not follow that every man written about, or writing, was faultless, and the record of their failings is no argument against the inspiration of the books. All that inspiration requires is that such things be set down as they are. He wants human nature seen as it is, and takes one purpose of these records to be the exhibiting of what a man is even under the influence of religion — not perfect, since that would be false, but mixed. So the wishes of ancient saints may stand in scripture condemned by the spirit of the religion that records them, never commended, only shown.

He then offers two ways many of the petitions may be innocent after all. Some were uttered by a public man, a magistrate, against robbers and the violent: if it is right that crime be detected and punished, and good men work for it, there is nothing improper in praying that the laws be executed, and this may be done with no spirit of revenge at all. Others were simply predictions of what sin brings and what God will do — which is how the apostle takes this one, and in a prediction, Barnes says, there can be nothing wrong.
11:
The objection is again put in an adversary's mouth, and Gill makes its edge felt. If the nation's stumbling at Christ was foretold and appointed, what was God's end in it? Was it that they should fall and perish everlastingly? Then is he not doing what he forbids in others, laying a stumbling block before the blind (Leviticus 19:14), and how is he clear of cruelty? Or, granting the stumble was permitted, must they lie where they fell? Barnes puts the question doctrinally — is it God's design that they be irrecoverably cast off? — and answers from the two verbs. To stumble is to strike the foot against an obstacle and be checked in walking, at worst put in danger of falling; to fall is to pitch over it beyond recovery. Robertson notes the first verb appears only here in Paul and was probably suggested by the trap-word two verses back, and warns that much depends on whether the conjunction is taken as purpose, so that the sense would be merely that they might fall.

Calvin supplies the key he thinks the argument turns on. Paul speaks now of the nation as a whole and now of individuals, and unless the shift is watched he will seem to contradict himself, banishing the Jews from the kingdom in one place and denying they have fallen from grace in another. Read so, the two hold together: those who stumbled at Christ did fall into destruction, but the nation had not fallen, so that being a Jew does not entail perishing. He denies the covenant was abolished, since the seed of blessing always remained in that people, and observes that a hope of rising is offered here where before ruin was tied to blindness.

What the fall accomplished is stated without hesitation, and how it accomplished it is where the witnesses part. Barnes lists the ways the rejection opened the door: it broke down the standing barrier, it made the sending of the message elsewhere fitting once it had been refused, it went with the destruction of the temple and so taught that worship was tied to no one place, it scattered Jewish believers and carried the gospel with them, and it gave the apostles a clear view of what the Mosaic institutions were for — a lesson they learned slowly as it was, and would have learned far more slowly had the temple stood. Clarke refuses the causal reading altogether. The calling of the Gentiles was God's purpose from the first, implied in the covenant with Abraham, and would have stood whether Israel believed or not; unbelief in one people could never produce faith in another. What the Jews' obstinacy did was accelerate what was already resolved — the apostles turned, the Gentiles heard and believed, and the Jews, seeing others put in possession of their privileges, could not bear it. Calvin agrees that the purpose was not ruin but provocation, and hears behind the phrase the old threat of Moses, that God would answer their jealousy of him with a jealousy of their own. He renders the feeling exactly — what stirs in us when another is preferred before us — and illustrates it, as the passage invites, by a wife put away for her fault who is moved by the sight of her successor to seek reconciliation. Wesley catches the same lightness in the noun, calling it a slip, a very soft word in the original. Ellicott finds the cause of the apathy in the privileges themselves, which had made them negligent, and the cure in watching others step into them. Theodoret keeps to the history: the gospel was carried to them first, and only when they set themselves against it was it offered to the nations — a sequence framed to sting the gainsayers by letting them see the last made first.
12:
Clarke opens with a warning about the English. The word rendered fall here is not the word so rendered in the previous verse, and the difference is the argument. The earlier verb, he says, carries terrible force in Greek — Homer uses it twice of men going down in battle, over Patroclus slain and where the weapons flew thick — and to fall in battle is to be killed. That is the ruinous and irrecoverable fall Paul has just denied. The noun here is the softer word for a lapse or an offence, the same used of Adam's, and it names a fall a man can be raised from. Gill settles the other term: the world means the Gentiles, since the Jews called themselves the church and all the nations about them the world.

The sentence argues from the smaller to the greater, and Calvin states why the argument was needed. Gentiles might come to dislike the prospect of Jewish salvation if they supposed their own standing depended on Jewish ruin, so Paul heads the notion off with its opposite: nothing would advance them more than that grace should abound among the Jews. The first exchange, he adds, ran against nature, and the second will run with it. Nor will he grant that the gospel needed the refusal to reach the nations: had the Jews received it, their faith would have borne far more fruit than their unbelief occasioned, and many would have been led in by their teaching whom their perverseness turned aside. He breaks off with an apology for the plainness of his own comment, on the ground that these things were written to mould the heart and not the tongue.

The two nouns are set as opposites, and Ellicott hears a military figure under the first: the reduction of a people to a small remnant, as after a defeat. Against it he sets the other as the full complement of the nation, its restoration so complete that not one is missing and every Jew is a member of the Messianic kingdom. Barnes traces the word through its ordinary uses — what fills a vessel, the patch that fills a rent (Matthew 9:16), the fragments left at the feeding, love as the filling up of the law — and lands on the same sense, a complete recovery from unbelief.

What such a recovery would mean is where Barnes becomes concrete, and he grounds it on what the nation already is rather than on prophecy. They are scattered through all nations and have access to every people. Their conversion, after unbelief so long, would carry the force of a miracle done in view of the world, and would show at last why they had been preserved. They know the languages, so that their turning would place missionaries at once in the heart of every kingdom, lighting a thousand lamps in dark places. And they have shown themselves fitted for the work, since the gospel was first spread by Jews and every one of the apostles was one; the zeal and enterprise of the nation, he thinks, have not been lost. Wesley is more confident still. So many prophecies bear on this event that he finds it surprising any Christian doubts it, and takes the survival of the Jews as a distinct people to be a standing confirmation; when it comes it will demonstrate both Testaments so strongly as to convince thousands settled into unbelief in nominally Christian countries, and will carry the gospel swiftly to Muslims and heathen — who, he adds pointedly, would probably have received it long ago had they only met real Christians. Theodoret makes the same point without the forecast: if a believing minority brought the riches of divine knowledge to the nations, all the more would the whole, when those who now oppose join instead in the preaching.
13:
The address narrows, and Gill explains why it can. The Roman church, like most of the first churches, held Jews and Gentiles together, so Paul turns from one to the other as his argument requires; here he turns to the Gentiles to remind them whose gospel enriched them, and to keep them from despising the people it came out from. Clarke would set this verse and the next in a parenthesis, reading them as an aside in which the apostle spreads the height of Gentile privilege before them for two purposes at once — that they may feel what mercy called them, and be jealous over themselves lest they fall as the Jews fell. Ellicott wants the punctuation and the particles reset by the amended text: the opening conjunction dropped, a full stop after the word Gentiles, spoken with something of a pause, and the next clause begun in so far then as. He hears the sentence as carrying a second thought behind the first — the motive at least partly to win over his own countrymen. Robertson confirms that the phrase is qualitative rather than temporal, so much as, not so long as.

Why the title belongs to Paul in particular is a fair question, since he was not the only one to cross that line, and Barnes answers it carefully. Other apostles preached to Gentiles, all of them but perhaps James, and Paul himself preached often enough in synagogues; the title is his because his original commission was to the nations (Acts 9:15), because his work was the gathering and ordering of churches in heathen lands, and because the charge of the Gentile churches fell to him as the Jewish churches fell to Peter. From that appointment he draws the authority to speak to them as he is about to.

The last clause is where the witnesses part, and the dispute is about a translation. Clarke calls the received rendering very improper: the Greek says I honour this my ministry, and in English to magnify anything but God carries the suggestion of stretching past the truth, whereas Paul is only doing his office justice by stating the glorious things he was sent to preach. Robertson renders it I glorify my ministry and adds the wish that every minister of Christ did. Calvin takes the verb in the sense he thinks scripture usually gives it, not to think highly of a thing but to make it illustrious, and reads the whole sentence as an argument that the two salvations are bound together: though specially charged with the Gentiles, and bound to labour for them almost to the exclusion of all else, Paul says he discharges that office faithfully when he gains any of his own nation to Christ, since this makes his ministry glorious and so serves the Gentiles too. His editor notes that some of the Latin fathers and Luther read the verb as a future — I shall render it glorious — which would ease the sentence, and suggests placing the clause about his apostleship in a parenthesis to clear the construction.

Barnes turns the phrase into a rule for ministers, and it depends on a distinction. A man may not magnify himself, but he may magnify his office; he may reckon himself less than the least of all saints and unworthy to be called a servant, and still know that he is an ambassador entrusted with a message of salvation and entitled to the respect that goes with the errand. Holding both together, Barnes says, is what the dignity of the ministry consists in. Wesley says it in a line: far from being ashamed of ministering to the Gentiles, he glories in it, the rather because it may provoke his brethren.
14:
The aim behind the boasting is stated at last, and Gill puts it plainly: all the labour and assiduity Paul spent among the Gentiles had this in view, that he might stir his own people to imitate them in seeking Christ. Theodoret ties the two halves of the ministry together in one motion — sent as minister to the nations, he necessarily labours for their salvation, directs his discourse on their behalf and shows the old prophets foretelling it, and by that very work excites the Jews to rivalry so that some may share the salvation. He also glosses the word Paul uses for his countrymen: he calls them his flesh because in spirit they stood at a distance, related to him only by the tie of kindred. Barnes gives the same word its ordinary scriptural range, countrymen or kinsmen, those of one family or nation.

How the provoking was to be done is where Barnes becomes interesting, because the means he describes are unwelcome. Paul expected to work on them by unpleasant truths — by pressing the ancient prophecies, by alarming them about their own danger, by holding up the privileges the Gentiles now enjoyed under the gospel — and Barnes notes the paradox that no doctrine could be more likely to irritate and offend than the one he was preaching, that the nation would be cast off, and yet he used it faithfully in hope of saving some. From this Barnes draws a short theory of how such preaching works. Truth often irritates and enrages, and by irritating excites attention; thought once excited, however it was excited, may end in conversion; so even restlessness and vexation and anger may be the road by which a man comes to Christ.

He immediately fences the observation about, and the fence is as firm as the point. It is no part of a minister's object to produce anger. Anger is a bad emotion and evil in itself, and if men can be won without it, that is better; no wise man raises a storm he may then need infinite power to quiet, when the same end could be reached under the mild influence of love. What Barnes does defend is the breadth of means. It is right to use every method not positively wicked in order to save men; Paul, he says, was full of devices, and much of the ministry's success will turn on a wise choice of plans that God may bless to the arresting of souls.

The modesty of the expected result is noticed on all sides. Paul hopes to save some, and Clarke draws the consequence for the doctrine of the chapter: these were all among the rejected, and yet the apostle plainly supposed that none of them were irrecoverably shut out from the divine favour, and that some might be brought by his preaching to receive salvation through Christ. Calvin stops instead at the verb, since it is startling to hear a man say he saves anyone. He allows the expression and then hedges it on both sides: the minister of the word is in some way said to save those he brings to the obedience of faith, so the ministry of our salvation ought to be so conducted that we feel the whole power and efficacy of it to depend on God and give him the praise; and at the same time we should understand that preaching really is the instrument by which the faithful are saved, and that though it can do nothing without the Spirit of God, it produces the most powerful effects through his inward working.
15:
The argument runs again from the smaller case to the greater, and Gill marks what is being reasoned from: the casting away is God writing Lo-ammi over that people and taking the gospel from them, and if the Gentiles gained by that, they will gain more by the recovery — which is itself proof that the rejection is not final. Barnes settles the middle term. Reconciliation is properly the pacifying of parties at variance, and it is the word the New Testament uses for what Christ effects between God and men, so that the ministry itself is named from it. Jewish unbelief opened the way for that message to go to the nations.

The last three words are the difficulty, and the commentators divide over whether they are a figure or a forecast. Barnes reads a figure, and explains the need for one from the shape of Paul's own sentences. He had already said that the rejection reconciled the world and made the riches of the Gentiles; to say now that the recovery would convert the world would be insipid and tame, so he reaches for the most tremendous image available. The resurrection of the dead stands for the greatest change conceivable, and Barnes takes it to mean the recovery of the nations from the death of sin, not any literal rising — the same figure the prophet used of a people in a state of ruin (Ezekiel 37:1). Calvin argues the same way and is sharper about the alternative, calling the passage one that many find obscure and some awfully pervert. His test is the balance of the sentence: since the rejection of the Jews was reconciliation to the Gentiles, the receiving of the Jews must be life from the dead to the Gentiles too, so the phrase describes a revival of religion in a decayed Gentile world rather than the resurrection at the end. He names the reading he is rejecting, that of Chrysostom and Theodoret, and calls it wholly at variance with the context. Wesley agrees in four words — overflowing life to a world that was dead.

Theodoret's own account is exactly what Calvin describes. If the nations were brought in on Jewish unbelief, then were all of these willing to believe, nothing would remain to be accomplished but the resurrection of the dead; and he grounds it on the saying that the gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness, and then shall the end come (Matthew 24:14). He adds that Paul argues so to teach humility to the believing Gentiles while holding the offer open to the Jews. Ellicott takes the same side without argument, treating the reconversion as the signal inaugurating the reign of eternal life which the resurrection ushers in. Robertson leaves the question open and reports the state of it: many think Paul means the general resurrection and the end will come when the Jews are converted, which is possibly so but by no means certain, and the language may be merely figurative. He also observes, as a man of his own time, that the conversion of Jews had already become so difficult that it looked like a miracle of grace whenever it happened.

What such a recovery would do is where Clarke and Barnes agree. Clarke asks the Gentile reader to want it as he would want a much-loved friend back from the gates of death, and treats their survival as a distinct people as collateral proof that it will come; when it does, the fulfilment of prophecies delivered so long before will convert multitudes who now deny revelation, and a whole nation may be born as in a day. Barnes says the same: scattered everywhere, with access to all peoples and their languages, their conversion would kindle a thousand lights at once in the darkness.
16:
Two images make one argument, and the first is a rite. Barnes explains that a portion of the harvest, and specifically a small cake of the kneaded dough, was separated and presented to God before the rest could lawfully be used (Numbers 15:19); the part offered rendered the mass lawful, so that consecrating a little consecrated all. Ellicott adds the ceremony: the piece taken was a heave offering, waved before the Lord and then given to the priest. Calvin distinguishes the two firstfruits the law knew — the sheaf of first ripe grain and the first kneaded cake — and identifies the second as the one meant here. Robertson notes that the Greek phrase follows the wording of that same law.

Who the firstfruit is turns out to be the real question. Gill reports the reading that takes both figures of Christ, who is called the firstfruits of them that slept and the root of Jesse, and grants that since he is holy those who have their sanctification in him must be holy too; but he sets it aside as not agreeing with the apostle's argument here. He is harder on the second reading, which makes the firstfruit the Jewish ancestors and dreams of a holiness running down from Abraham to his natural seed: if no such holiness reached his immediate son Ishmael, it can hardly have reached a posterity four or five thousand years off. His own answer is the early Jewish converts, on the ground that Paul habitually calls the first believers in any place the firstfruits of it. Clarke takes both at once, the conversion of Abraham and of the Jews who have now embraced Christianity, and defines the word carefully — holy here means consecrated, set apart to sacred use, in the sense the Old Testament gives it constantly. Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott settle on the patriarchs, Robertson venturing that the root may be Abraham singly and reminding the reader of the double sense of Israel running through these chapters; Barnes hears behind the second image the prophet's picture of the nation as a green olive tree, fair and of goodly fruit (Jeremiah 11:16).

Calvin's concern is that the holiness not be mistaken for a personal one. He begins by levelling the comparison — nation against nation, not man against man, since Jew and Gentile are equally the children of Adam and the only difference is that one was separated to be a peculiar people. The conclusion that hereditary holiness passed from the patriarchs to the whole race would be false if it were said of persons, for a just father cannot transmit his uprightness to his son; it holds because God sanctified Abraham to this very end, that his seed should be holy, conferring the thing not on a person but on a race. That the holiness meant is external and relative rather than inward is plain, he says, from the whole context, since the children of Israel are called holy in the middle of their disobedience. His editors press the point with cases: Pareus observes that the worst often descend from the best and the best from the worst, from Ahaz came Hezekiah, from Hezekiah came Manasseh, from Manasseh came Josiah, and from Josiah came sons who were wicked — yet all alike were holy in the sense meant, being circumcised and heirs of the covenant's transferable rights. Calvin closes by conceding that the Jews may truly be called naturally holy, their adoption being hereditary, while insisting that our first nature leaves us all accursed in Adam, so that the dignity of an elect people is strictly a supernatural privilege. Wesley reads the whole verse forward rather than backward: the consecration of the firstfruits was reckoned the consecration of all, and the conversion of a few Jews is the earnest of the conversion of the rest.
17:
Gill begins by limiting what the breaking off means, and his reason is chronological. It cannot be exclusion from their national church, since the men chiefly meant — the rulers, the priests, the scribes and Pharisees and the bulk of the people — were that church, while the apostles and followers of Christ were the ones being put out of the synagogues. Nor can it be the destruction of the nation and the temple, for when Paul wrote, the nation stood and Jerusalem stood and the temple stood. What it means is their being left outside the gospel church gathered among them, after they had rejected the Messiah and then contradicted the preaching, until it pleased God to take the gospel wholly away from them.

Barnes fills in the horticulture, quoting a description of the tree: the cultivated olive of moderate height, knotty trunk, smooth ash-coloured bark, solid yellowish wood and long willow-like leaves, and the wild olive smaller in every part and, by the old writers' account, barren. The figure then reads itself. The stock is ancient and good, the branches had decayed and been removed, and a shoot from the barren kind was set in and drew the rich sap of the root, so that a fruitless church became vigorous. Robertson supplies the technical terms, including the verb for cutting in a graft, which Aristotle already used, and notes the three genitives Paul stacks up — of the root, of the fatness, of the olive.

Whether the operation described is real gardening is a genuine dispute. Robertson reports Ramsay's finding that the ancients did graft a wild-olive shoot onto an old olive tree in order to reinvigorate it, exactly as the figure supposes, and that stock and graft influenced each other, though the fruit of the wild graft never equalled the original; but he sets against this that Paul himself calls the procedure contrary to nature a few verses on. Calvin does not think it happens at all except where the good tree is failing, and does not think it matters: the apostle's object was not to describe what is usual but to frame a comparison fit for his purpose, as Christ sometimes did in the parables. What Paul has done, Calvin points out, is invert nature, making the stock good and the graft bad and letting the stock improve the graft's fruit rather than the reverse. Wesley makes the inversion the whole force of the warning: even had the graft been nobler than the stock, its dependence on it for life and nourishment would leave it no room to boast, and how much less when, against all human practice, the wild olive is grafted into the good.

Calvin also notices how carefully the severity is moderated. Paul does not say the top of the tree was cut off but that some of the branches were broken, and that God took Gentiles here and there and set them in the blessed trunk — which leaves the Gentiles nothing to glory in over the Jews, since whatever standing they have comes from the new insertion and not from the old stock, their own race having had nothing in it but a curse. The one phrase he cannot settle is where the new branches were put. His own rendering is in their stead, and Beza, Pareus and Macknight agree; Grotius has between them and Doddridge among them. Ellicott prefers the last, taking it of the branches generally, both those broken off and those left standing, while allowing that in place of them is possible. He also reports a textual question in the closing phrase: three of the weightiest manuscripts omit the second connective, which would give the root of the fatness, and make the sense that the rich flow of sap the wild olive shares in belongs not to it but wholly to the root.
18:
The warning follows directly from the graft, and Robertson hears in the verb that the fault was already present. The imperative is not a caution against a possible sin but a command to stop a habitual one — do not go on glorying over the branches — and the pronoun that follows sits in a very emphatic position: not thou. He allows the qualification his horticulture required, that the graft was set on the stock and root even though each affected the other.

What forbids the boast is the direction the sap runs. Ellicott states it in a line: there can be no glorying, because the privileges the Gentiles hold are derived and not original. Clarke turns it toward the very people being despised — you have not been the means of bringing any blessing on the Jewish people, but through that very people all the blessings you enjoy have been communicated to you. Barnes states it as a matter of arithmetic in the figure: if there were ground for boasting anywhere it would be in the root that sustains the branches, and least of all in a shoot grafted in which was unfruitful before. He then draws out what the image commits Paul to, which is more than a caution. The apostle plainly regards the church as one, and the Christian dispensation as a prolongation of the old one, for a tree keeps its identity when branches are removed and others put in, and is never afterwards reckoned a different tree.

Calvin makes the same point by naming the person the Gentiles would be quarrelling with. They could not contend with the Jews about the excellence of their race without contending with Abraham, who is the root that bears and feeds them, and that would be as unreasonable as branches boasting against the root; so Paul would have them keep in view where their salvation came from. He adds the historical fact that gives the figure its force — that when Christ pulled down the partition wall the whole world came into a favour that had been conferred beforehand on a chosen people, so that the calling of the Gentiles was itself an ingrafting, and they grew as God's people only as they were set into Abraham's stock.

Theodoret supplies a key to the whole allegory, and it is the one place the terms are all assigned at once: by the firstfruit he understands Christ in his human nature, by the root the patriarch Abraham, by the branches the Jewish people sprung from him, and by the richness of the olive the doctrines of religion. On that reading the admonition is that men born of another race have been grafted into this one and have received of the fatness of a holy root; and he presses the reversal twice over, that the root bears you and not you the root, and that you need it and it does not need you.

Two of the witnesses turn the caution into something more than restraint. Gill will not have the Gentile merely refrain from vaunting over those broken off, but have him pity them and pray for them, and be thankful and humbled under a sense of the grace that settled him — himself once comparable to a wild olive — in a gospel church; still less may he glory over the believing Jews among whom he sits, there being no difference at all, since they are one in Christ. Wesley makes it a question with an edge on it, and aims it past the first century: do not those do this very thing who despise the Jews, or who deny their future conversion?
19:
A voice is put into the Gentile's mouth, and the commentators agree on its tone. Robertson calls the speaker presumptuous and hears contempt for the cast-off Jews in the very shape of the sentence, which makes the breaking off exist for the sake of the grafting. Barnes reconstructs the reasoning behind it fairly: from what Paul had said two paragraphs earlier, it does look as though the rejection of the ancient people were the means of opening the church to the nations, and if that is so a Gentile might feel he had some ground for exulting. Clarke states it more bluntly still — God was displeased with them, cast them out, and took you in their place. What Barnes then anticipates is the answer: that this was not why they were rejected, unbelief was.

Calvin takes the plea and turns it round. Granting everything the objector says, what follows from it? If the cutting off was through unbelief and the grafting in was by faith, then the Gentile's proper business is to acknowledge a favour and to keep his mind modest and low, since it belongs to the nature of faith to generate humility and fear. He renders the coming warning literally — not be not high-minded but be not elated in mind — and is careful about the fear that answers it. It is not a fear at odds with the assurance of faith; Paul would not have faith vacillate or alternate with doubt, still less have us quake. His account of it depends on holding two things in view at once, since God bids us remember the misery of our own nature, which can yield nothing but dread and weariness and anxiety, and it is expedient that we be laid prostrate so that we may groan to him — yet that dread, drawn from knowing ourselves, does not keep the mind from resting calm on his goodness, and that weariness does not bar full consolation, and that anxiety does not prevent real joy and hope. So the fear is set up as an antidote against proud contempt, because every man claims more than his share and grows secure and at length insolent, and we ought to fear just so far as keeps the heart from swelling.

The obvious objection is that such a warning throws salvation itself into doubt, and Calvin answers it with a distinction he will lean on for the rest of the chapter. The exhortation is aimed at subduing the flesh, which stays insolent even in God's children, so it takes nothing from the certainty of faith; and the address is not to individuals but to the whole body of the Gentiles, among whom there were many inflated men professing faith rather than possessing it. It is on their account that excision is threatened. His editors press the same point against a reading they think has been built on this verse — that faith may be uncertain and may fail — calling it an entire misapprehension of the subject: what is in view is the Gentile world and not the individual, professed faith and not living, outward privilege and not inward change, union with the Church and not union of the soul with Christ, and to argue from the one to the other is illegitimate. They cite Augustine, who found in the promise to put fear in men's hearts that they might not depart a promise of perseverance itself, and Pareus, whose rule is that those who believe for a time never had true faith however it looked, while those who have it never fail, God infallibly sustaining them.
20:
The reply opens with a word of assent, and how much assent it carries is disputed. Robertson thinks it perhaps ironical, while allowing that Paul may simply be granting the statement in order to show the Gentile where he actually stands. Barnes reads it as a piece of argumentative tact worth studying: the main force of the remark is admitted, then given a slight turn in the direction of the truth, so that the objection's own weight is made to carry the point Paul wanted to press. Gill describes the same manoeuvre from the other side — the breaking off and the grafting are granted, and what is quietly denied is that the one happened for the sake of the other. It happened because of unbelief.

The two datives are set opposite each other, and Robertson notes that both are instrumental: by unbelief broken off, by faith standing. Clarke works the consequence out in a chain. If the blessings were received by faith, then not by works; if not by works, then there is no merit anywhere in the transaction, and what you have is the mere mercy of God — so this ought to humble rather than exalt you. He then makes the parallel exact and uncomfortable: they once stood by faith, gave place to unbelief and fell; you stand now by faith, and it is as possible for you to be unfaithful as it was for them. Wesley fastens on the same conditionality and says why it matters — both clauses are conditional and not absolute, since had they been absolute there would have been room to boast — and adds that the faith itself is God's free gift, which is a second reason for humility rather than a first for pride. Theodoret puts it as a simple exchange: unbelief made them aliens from the root, faith connected you with it and gave you its richness, so it becomes you not to grow self-sufficient but to fear and tremble.

What the fear is meant to be gets the most careful handling. Barnes will not let it mean terror or horror; it stands opposed to the boasting and self-confidence he has been arguing against, and he defines it as humility, watchfulness, and solicitude to abide in the faith. He quotes an account of the posture wanted — not haughtiness against a Jew who has been cast off, but the bearing of a humble believer who knows he must be continually on his guard lest he too fall through unbelief. Clarke calls it a godly jealousy exercised over oneself. Barnes draws three lessons and they follow one another. There is a real danger that men raised to eminent privileges will think too well of themselves and too little of others. The tendency of faith runs the opposite way, toward humility and a sense of dependence on God. And a system of salvation by faith produces exactly the watchfulness needed to keep a man from apostasy, which is why the warning is not at odds with the doctrine but grows out of it.

Barnes states the practical upshot without hedging it. The continuance of these mercies depends on fidelity: if the Gentile churches remain faithful the mercies will be preserved, and if they become unbelieving and unfruitful as the Jews did, they will be rejected as the Jews were. That prospect, he says, is what ought to repress boasting and put anxiety and caution in its place.
21:
The warning is turned into an argument from the greater case to the smaller, and Gill spells out what made the Jews the greater. They were the natural descendants of Abraham, born as they stood into a national church state and into the covenant God made with that people; a national adoption belonged to them, so that they were called his sons and his firstborn; they were chosen out as a peculiar people for very great privileges; and Christ was their own, come of them according to the flesh and sent particularly to them, and ministering among them. If after so long forbearance God did not spare a people holding all that, when they disbelieved his Son and despised the salvation offered in him, then the Gentiles in a church state have every reason to be careful. Barnes states the same inference in a sentence and adds the point that stings: it may be supposed that God will be quite as ready to reject a grafted branch as one belonging to the parent stock, so the Gentile's position gives him no security whatever over the Jew's.

Robertson translates the opening command as a demand to stop something already happening — stop thinking high thoughts — and notes that the condition is of the kind assumed to be true, the negative attaching to the verb of sparing rather than to the clause. Ellicott raises the text of the second half, judging it better to drop the words rendered take heed lest, which leaves the flatter and harder statement that neither will he spare you.

Calvin calls this the most powerful thing yet said against self-confidence, and describes the effect it should have physically: the rejection of the Jews ought never to cross our minds without striking and shaking us. He puts the diagnosis of their ruin in one clause — that through supine dependence on the dignity they had obtained they despised what God appointed — and asks what will be done to men who are wild olive and aliens if they grow arrogant beyond measure. Then he turns the same thought the other way, since a consideration that makes us distrust ourselves also makes us cleave more firmly to the goodness of God. He also takes the verse as further evidence for the reading he has been urging, that the address is to the body of the Gentiles rather than to individuals, on the ground that excision cannot touch men whose election is unchangeable and rests on God's eternal purpose. What is being told the Gentiles is that if they exult over the Jews a reward is being prepared for their pride, and that God will yet reconcile to himself the people he has divorced.

Clarke presses the same warning into self-examination, telling the Gentile to remember the rock he was hewn from and the pit he was dug out of, and to depend without ceasing on free grace if he means to abide in favour; the righteous principle that acted once will act again if men sin after the same pattern, and self-sufficiency is the shortest road to that. Wesley guards the fear from being mistaken, in a line as compact as the definition needs to be: it is not opposed to trust, but to pride and security. Theodoret makes the argument turn on character rather than descent — the connection of nature profited them nothing once they no longer kept the same disposition, and much more shall you become a stranger to the root if you do not keep the grace given.
22:
Barnes insists the second noun has been misheard. Severity now suggests harshness or even cruelty, but the Greek word is built on a verb meaning to cut off and belongs to the gardener trimming a tree of its decayed branches; used of God's dealing with the Jews it conveys no idea of injustice, however heavy the consequences. Robertson confirms the derivation and notes the word stands here alone in the New Testament though it turns up in the papyri. Gill takes the pairing itself to be the lesson: holding grace toward some and strict justice toward others in one view is what abates pride.

Clarke turns the metaphor into a manual, writing as a man who has done the work. He derives the word for grafting from the practice of puncturing the bark to insert a bud, quotes the passage in the Georgics that describes it, and sets out the operation as he has performed it himself — the branch cut back, the remainder slit, the scion shaved wedge-like, the joint bound and clayed until bark unites with bark and the stock's sap circulates through the new twig. Paul's two nouns are then the halves of one gardener's action, goodness the insertion and severity the cutting back. The tree was cut down but not rooted up; and since the Gentile branch draws its life from the Abrahamic covenant, its standing is bound up with the survival of the people through whom that covenant came. The restoration, he adds, need not come at Gentile expense, the original stock being sufficient for all.

Barnes examines the condition attached to the goodness, noting that the possessive in his goodness is not in the Greek and that the noun can equally mean probity, which he thinks likelier, so that the clause turns on conduct rather than on a state of favour. He states the balance precisely — Christians do not merit God's favour by faith and good works, but obedience is the indispensable condition of its continuing — and gives the cases: the seven churches of Asia, Corinth, Antioch, Philippi and Rome itself lost what they had. Robertson marks the closing verb as a plain future passive, cut out exactly as the Jewish branches were; Wesley makes it final.

Calvin dramatises the warning as a speech. Think first what you were, since the same severity would have hung over you but for a free favour; then what you are now, since salvation will not continue unless you keep recognising mercy. He then names the event that proved the warning necessary, and it is not the first century. God had watered the world with grace almost in a moment, religion flourishing everywhere, and soon after the gospel's truth vanished and the treasure of salvation was taken away — a defection he lays to the Gentiles falling from their calling. Since withering threatens everyone as far as nature goes, he holds that the warning reaches even the faithful, lest they indulge the sloth of the flesh.

Henry, observing that spiritual judgments are the sorest of all, argues the restoration from the harder case already granted: that Israel should be brought back is less improbable than that Gentiles should have been made children of Abraham at all, and that others now hold the privileges is no bar to their readmission. He is careful what it would mean — not priesthood and temple and ceremonies, to all of which an end has been put, but belief in Christ and one sheepfold with the Gentiles under one shepherd. Lightfoot, prefacing his own work on the chapter, raises a prior question that unsettles the usual chronology. The casting off of that nation is commonly dated from the murder of Christ, a wickedness that abundantly deserved it; but were they not blinded and cast off before that? They were a generation of vipers, he points out, when the Baptist first appeared.
23:
The condition is stated negatively, and Barnes takes that to be the whole hinge. Since unbelief was the sole cause of the rejection, the removal of unbelief removes the cause, and nothing then stands between them and restored favour. He reads the sentence as establishing two things at once: that God has the power to bring them back, and that he has not bound himself to exclude them for ever — which is precisely what was needed to answer the question the chapter opened with. Clarke reaches the same place with a different emphasis, that their rejection followed on wilful obstinacy and that the door still stands open. He presses the point about ability further than Barnes does: the wording intimates that God has furnished them with all the power and means necessary for faith, so that they may believe whenever they will, and the veil that now lies on their heart is not one God spread there but one their own obstinate unbelief occasioned, which will be taken away when they turn to the Lord.

Gill agrees the thing is possible and doubts it will happen unaided, and his hesitation is the sharpest note in the verse. They seem to him to lie under an ignorance nothing can overcome, obstinate, bitter against the gospel and its ordinances and against a gospel church state; and he goes further, saying they must and will abide in unbelief unless the Spirit of God convinces them, it is given them to believe, and they are powerfully drawn. The restoration is not denied — it is put wholly on the side of the God who would have to work it.

Which is where the last clause takes the argument. Robertson calls the statement that God is able the crux of the whole matter and lets it stand without elaboration. Calvin doubts it would persuade everyone, and explains why the appeal works only on some hearers. To the profane the argument is frigid, for though they concede God power they view it at a distance, shut up as it were in heaven, and so rob it of any effect; the faithful, hearing power named, look on it as presently at work, and for them the reason is enough. He adds that Paul takes an axiom for granted here — that God had punished the unbelief of his people without forgetting his mercy — and appeals to what had already happened more than once, the Jews restored after they seemed to have been banished from his kingdom.

Calvin also draws out the comparison hidden in the two graftings, and it is the point the next verse will make explicit. Reversing the present arrangement would be easier than establishing it was: for natural branches to be set back where they were cut from and draw sap from their own root is a smaller thing than for wild and unfruitful ones to draw it from a stock not theirs. Theodoret makes the same symmetry a matter of justice rather than ease. It becomes God's righteousness both ways — to sever again the man who was blessed with a root beyond all hope, if he does not keep the grace given, and to join the others back to it if they renounce their unbelief. He notes with approval that the same word for grafting is used of the Jews as of the Gentiles, since unbelief had severed them exactly as faith connects.
24:
The comparison rests on the barrenness of one tree, and Clarke assembles the evidence that it was proverbial. The Greeks had a saying, more unfruitful than the wild olive; a lexicographer glosses the very word Paul uses by the word for fruitless; another collector of proverbs explains the phrase by stating flatly that the wild olive is an unfruitful tree; and Clarke notes the Spartan name for it that lies behind the proverb. From this he draws a point about the phrase describing it.
