The words rendered by nature do not mean that the tree is naturally barren so much as that it is customarily left uncultivated, and he takes the following clause to prove it, since the corresponding phrase there means contrary to all custom — a scion from a barren or useless tree being scarcely ever grafted into a good stock, which is exactly what has happened here. Robertson keeps the other half of the sense, that the whole point is God's power to do what natural processes do not do, and supplies the technical name for the garden olive that stands opposite the wild one. Wesley states the inversion in a sentence: by nature the fruitful branch is grafted into the wild stock, and here the wild branch is grafted into the fruitful.

What the inversion is meant to prove is an argument from the harder case to the easier. Barnes states it as such: reclaiming the Gentiles and turning them from enmity to friendship was in itself as difficult as making a wild olive fruitful, and if God did that, will he not much rather do the lesser thing for a people who had the promises, the covenants and the law, whose ancestors were his friends, and among whom the Messiah was born? He also insists the figure is not a claim about physical constitution. To say the Gentiles were grafted contrary to nature means contrary to their own habits, thoughts and practices, there having been among them no tendency toward God, not that they were depraved in the manner of a tree.

Barnes then descends from the argument to the facilities, listing what a Jewish hearer already has that a heathen one did not. They worship one God. They admit the authority of revelation. They hold the Scriptures of the Old Testament. They expect a Messiah. And they have a settled habit of professed reverence for the will of God. Clarke argues from the same asymmetry and puts the Gentile side at its lowest, quoting the description of men who were without God and atheists in the world (Ephesians 2:12): if such a change was possible in them, how much more, speaking after the manner of men, in a people who acknowledge the one true God and receive the law and the prophets as his revelation. This, he says, is the drift of the whole argument.

Theodoret makes the contrast concrete by naming what the wild olive lacked. You had no law tending you, he says, and no prophets watering and pruning and taking the needful care of you; you were detached from unholy ancestors and made a partaker in Abraham's faith, and boast in him as your father, not by any natural course of the law but by the divine kindness. If that could be done, it must be far more probable and more natural that men whose root it actually is should be united to it again on believing. He adds his standing account of why Paul argues so — to teach humility to the Gentiles who had believed, and to hold the offer open to the Jews who had not. Gill reads the sequence the same way, taking the previous verse to argue the restoration from God's power and this one to argue its likelihood from what has already been done in the Gentiles.
25:
What kind of thing a mystery is gets settled before its content is stated. Barnes insists the word carries no suggestion of something unintelligible: it means what had been concealed and is now disclosed, and the doctrine so named is commonly plain once told. Ellicott says the same from the other side: in Paul the word never means something withheld from all but a few, but a truth previously hidden and now made manifest by the gospel, applied sometimes to the whole Christian system and sometimes to a part. Robertson is emphatic that the pagan sense is absent — not an esoteric doctrine for initiates or anything like the mystery religions of the age, but a revealed will of God made known to all — and passes on the observation that the early Latin rendering of the word by sacramentum generated a whole mistaken account of the term. Clarke goes to the etymology, deriving it from a Hebrew root meaning to hide while noting that others trace it to a Greek verb for being initiated; here it means the future restoration of the Jews, unknown in itself and wholly unknown as to when. Theodoret defines it as a thing known only to those entrusted with it.

Calvin adds the pastoral reason for revealing it. Paul rouses his hearers because he means to settle a perplexed question briefly, and because what he is about to say is what nobody expected; the disclosure both checks Gentile arrogance and keeps the defection of the Jews from unsettling weak minds, as though that whole people were to be despaired of. He presses the use of it: when a long delay tempts us to despair we should remember that the manner of their conversion will be neither common nor usual, so that measuring it by our own judgment is absurd. On the warning against self-conceit, he takes the phrase from the proverb about being wise in one's own eyes and reads it as a caution against being elated over newly acquired privilege. Wesley names two forms that conceit takes: dreaming you are the only church, or that the church of Rome cannot fail.

The qualifying phrase is read three ways. Robertson attaches it to the verb: the hardening has happened partly. Ellicott attaches it to Israel, so that the hardness extends over some and not all, and points to the Jewish converts in Rome itself. Calvin denies it refers either to time or to number and makes it mean in a manner or in a measure, a softening of a hard declaration; his editor rejects that, holding that extent and duration are both plainly meant, since the term is given a limit in the very next clause. Barnes reads it as partial and no more, deliberately silent about which part and for how long.

How full the fulness must be is the practical question. Calvin takes it for a great number, on the ground that the change was to be such that Gentiles would form almost the whole body of the Church. Clarke resists any reading that makes the restoration wait on an absolute completion. The word need not mean every nation and every individual in them, but may mean a general spread of Christianity through many lands now under other faiths; nor need the coming in mean what is usually understood by conversion, since acknowledging Christ's mission and cordially embracing his religion satisfies the words. His warning is blunt: wait for the Jews until every Gentile and every Muslim soul is converted in that stricter sense, and we shall wait for ever. Barnes reaches a similar result by another route: Paul does not say the Jews must wait on the completion of the Gentile mission, having already said their conversion would help it forward, so the two are likely intermingled and perhaps simultaneous, and Christians may work for both at once.
26:
Everything turns on two words, and the commentators divide over them as sharply as anywhere in the chapter. Gill states the reading he rejects first: many take Israel here for the mystical Israel made of Jews and Gentiles together. His own view is the people of the Jews, the body of that nation, and he describes what he expects in the language of the prophets — a nation born again at once, coming up out of the lands where they were scattered, appointing themselves one head, seeking the Lord their God and David their king, and acknowledging Jesus as the true Messiah. Calvin takes the opposite side and takes it deliberately. He extends the word to all the people of God: when the Gentiles come in, the Jews will return from their defection, and so the salvation of the whole Israel of God will be completed out of both — though with the Jews holding first place, as the firstborn in the family. He appeals to the phrase used at the close of Galatians for the church gathered alike from Jews and Gentiles, and thinks this reading suits Paul's purpose, which was to set out the completion of a kingdom not to be confined to one nation. Robertson lays both options out and declines to choose. The immediate context, with its contrasts of part and whole, argues for the Jewish people as a body; the wider argument, which has twice distinguished two senses of Israel, may point to the spiritual Israel; and what he will commit to is that we should strive and pray for the conversion of Jews as a whole.

What saved means is a second question, and Clarke separates it from the first. The word here cannot mean eternal glory, since no one can seriously suppose that every Jew then living will be taken into it; applied to that people in scripture it regularly means being gathered out of the nations, separated to God, and put in possession of the privilege of being his peculiar people. Barnes divides the same way and adds the rabbinic maxim Paul is turning to his own use, that every Israelite has a portion in the age to come — true, Barnes says, of the nation and not of each man of every generation, since he has just finished proving that a great many were rejected. He also observes what the passage does not tell us. When this shall be is among the things the Father has kept in his own power, and Barnes reads the concealment as deliberate, given so that we should not relax our efforts in the belief that a fixed date will do the work without us.

The quotation is not exact, and the variation is itself discussed. Ellicott calls it a curious change: the prophet says the Redeemer shall come to Zion, the Greek version for the sake of Zion, and Paul out of Zion — which he explains as quoting from memory under the influence of other passages, adding the observation that the Messiah must first take up his abode there before he can issue from it. Barnes reports the same divergence, noting that the Greek, the Aramaic and the Latin all read otherwise than Paul does, and glosses Zion as standing for the people of God, so that the Deliverer arises among them rather than coming as a foreigner. Robertson identifies the participle with the Hebrew figure of the kinsman-avenger and says Paul applies it to Jesus. Wesley makes the tense the whole point of his comment, and it is the shortest statement of the chapter's hope: the deliverer is come already, but not yet the full fruit of his coming.
27:
The second half of the citation does not come from where the first half came, and the commentators trace it differently. Barnes takes it as an abridgement of the new-covenant promise in Jeremiah, the substance of it condensed into the closing clause about taking sins away, and thinks Paul was expressing the general sense of promises so familiar to Jewish readers that no argument about them was needed. Calvin agrees and says why the addition was necessary at just this point: what had been said about the conversion of a people so stubborn might well have seemed incredible, and the stumbling block is removed by showing that the covenant itself included a free remission of sins — God would have nothing more to do with an apostate people until he had pardoned the crime of perfidy along with the rest. Ellicott traces the clause elsewhere, to the Greek of a passage in Isaiah where the same two elements appear, the taking of transgression from Jacob and the very formula about a covenant with them. Robertson renders the possessive strictly — the covenant that proceeds from me, God's own side of the arrangement — and marks what kind of deliverance is in view: not a political one but a religious and ethical one.

Clarke's contribution is to show how much has been left out. He prints the prophet's words at length, with the promise about the Spirit resting on them and the words not departing out of the mouth of their seed nor of their seed's seed for ever, so that the reader can see how greatly the quotation has been compressed. He also proposes a rearrangement of the passage, holding that these two verses should be read as a parenthesis, since the sentence about the mystery joins directly to the sentence about their being enemies for the Gentiles' sake. Then he does something none of the others do and collects the evidence: a list of some two dozen places in the prophets which seem to him to point to a restoration of the Jewish commonwealth to a higher condition than it has yet reached, running from the opening chapters of Isaiah through Ezekiel and the minor prophets.

Barnes is as concerned to say what the promise does not contain. It does not mean that the Redeemer will come in person and preach to them, nor that they will be restored to the land of their fathers; neither idea, he says, is in the words. What he does expect is a conversion worked as the conversion of Gentiles is worked, by human means and in connection with the prayers of God's people — and he finds a fitness in that, since the Gentiles would then be repaying the labour of the ancient Jews who preserved the scriptures and prepared the way for the Messiah, and both would have cause to rejoice at having helped in the same work. Gill draws the plainest inference from the word covenant: what God has promised in covenant will not be broken, so that the call and conversion of the Jews is not merely possible or probable but certain.

Theodoret uses the last clause to identify the remission meant. If the ordering of the law gave forgiveness of sins, the prophet's words would point there; but the law punishes those who transgress it, and this people stood always under that charge, so the forgiveness in view must be the one that arises from baptism. He then takes the disputed phrase of the previous verse in Calvin's direction rather than Gill's, understanding by all Israel those who believe, whether they descend from Israel naturally or are joined to him by the kinship of faith.
28:
One people is described twice over in a single sentence, and the two descriptions are held apart by the two prepositional phrases. Barnes sets the terms opposite each other deliberately: enemies answers to beloved, so that in one respect, as regards the gospel, they stand cast off and opposed to God, and in another, as regards the election, they are still regarded with interest and purposes of mercy. Robertson makes the grammatical observation that settles the sense of both — each adjective is passive, so they are treated as enemies because they rejected Christ exactly as the others are treated as loved — and that keeps the verse from saying anything about their disposition toward God at all.

Whose enemies they are is a question the commentators put explicitly. Calvin's editor collects the answers and weighs them: enemies of Paul and of the Church, say Grotius and Luther; enemies of the gospel, says Pareus; enemies of God, say others — and the parallel with beloved in the next clause is taken to favour the last, since it is God who loves them. Wesley refuses to choose and adds a third party, making them enemies to the gospel, to God, and to themselves, with the note that God permits this. Barnes takes it as opposition to God, defining the biblical use of the term as covering all who are not his friends.

The clause about the Gentiles' advantage is the hinge, and Calvin turns it into a rebuke. The worst thing about the Jews ought not to expose them to Gentile contempt, because their chief crime, unbelief, was itself the means by which the way to the gospel was opened for the Gentiles; they were blinded for a time by a providence that had the Gentiles in view. He is careful to add what the blinding did not cancel: God was not unmindful of the covenant made with their fathers, by which he testified that according to his eternal purpose he loved that nation. Clarke says the same in terms of privilege — the grace that has overturned their peculiarity by admitting the nations is exactly what they resent — while insisting that with respect to the original choosing they remain beloved for their forefathers' sake. Ellicott states the position as a whole in two strokes: they were suffered to fall into estrangement to make room for the Gentiles, and this does not abrogate God's original choice of them, who are still his beloved people for the sake of the patriarchs if not for their own.

Barnes then guards the sentence against two misreadings at once. It does not mean that God approves their conduct or has the same kind of affection for them that obedience would draw out, since he does not love a sinful character; a man may be regarded with deep interest by one who intends yet to show him mercy without his present character being approved. Nor does the promise rest on any merit in the fathers. It rests on a covenant God made, and it will not be forgotten because God does not forget covenants. And Barnes will not let the doctrine be turned into security for anybody, adding that no one has any guarantee of God's favour except by complying with the terms of his mercy, which are explicit — repent and believe. Theodoret puts the whole double relation as a movement of the eye. Looking at the Gentiles he was charged to teach, he counts these men enemies and hateful, since they do all in their power to injure them; turning to their forefathers, and remembering that God chose them out of the whole earth, he finds that on their account he loves even these.
29:
Gill settles which gifts are meant by elimination. Not the gifts of nature and providence — life, health, riches, honour — which God gives and takes away again, as he is said to have repented of making man and of setting up Saul, an expression he takes for a change in the course of providence and not in the counsel of God's mind. Nor the external gifts of the Spirit that qualify men for public service, since the parable of the talents shows those may be withdrawn. What remains is the special and spiritual grace given to God's elect in Christ before the world was. Barnes defines the noun as a benefit conferred purely as favour and not as reward, and takes the calling to be the act by which God invites men to himself, whether by revelation, by the gospel promises, or by his Spirit — always with the pledge that what is offered will be given.

The English word in the last clause misleads, and three witnesses correct it in the same direction. Barnes insists it says nothing about man's repentance but only that God does not change his purpose, and gathers the texts that state this of him elsewhere, beginning with the declaration that God is not a man that he should lie nor a son of man that he should repent (Numbers 23:19). Clarke defines repentance as applied to God as a change of purpose relative to declarations made subject to conditions, and refers the reader to the passage in Jeremiah where God explains that principle himself. Robertson is the most exact: the Greek word is built on a verb meaning to be sorry afterwards, not on the word for changing one's mind, so the statement is that God is not sorry for his gifts. Ellicott catches both senses in a phrase — not to be revoked or withdrawn, and not even to be regretted.

What the promise covers is disputed, and the dispute matters. Calvin restricts it, reading the two nouns as one idea, the gift of calling, and referring it to the adoption by which God took the posterity of Abraham into covenant, since that is the subject in hand; the point is that the common adoption of the whole nation, which might look for a time as though it had failed, has not been cut up by the roots. His editor objects to the amalgamation as neither desirable nor necessary, prefers to read Paul as ascending — first the free promises, then the calling they came from — and reports that others extend the terms much further, to faith, remission of sins, sanctification and perseverance, and to the inward calling rather than the outward one that often fails. He notes a corollary drawn from that wider reading: that no Gentile nation once favoured with God's gifts and calling will be wholly forsaken.

Theodoret reads the verse against all of this, and argues from cases. God does resume the blessings he gives when he sees ingratitude in those who received them. Saul is proof, having enjoyed the grace and been stripped of it; Solomon likewise, whose peace was taken after his transgression; and the Jews themselves, long under the prophets' fostering care and at that moment bereaved of it. He points out that Paul had just threatened the believing Gentiles in the same terms — if you continue in his goodness, otherwise you also shall be cut off — and so takes the sentence as an incitement addressed to the Jews rather than an unconditional guarantee. Barnes draws the opposite consequences: the promises will be fulfilled, God's people need not despond under persecution, and none who become his true friends are cast off, since to renew a soul and then leave it to ruin would suppose exactly the change of purpose the verse denies, and would make God capricious.
30:
The argument turns back on the readers themselves, and Gill fills in the period being appealed to. These are the times of ignorance, idolatry and superstition, when God suffered the nations for many hundreds of years to walk in their own ways, while the Jews were his favoured people, chosen above all others, separated from them, and furnished with his word and oracles, his judgments and his statutes. He dates the stretch as everything before the coming of the Messiah, when these people sat in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death, until Christ, who came to lighten the Gentiles, sent his gospel among them with great success. What their unbelief consisted in he describes as a range rather than a single error: some did not believe there was a God at all, or that there was but one, and the few who did could not say who he was, nor glorify him as God, nor pay him any true spiritual worship, while the far greater part held that there were many gods and served them.

Barnes reads the same clause as a plain reference to the former idolatrous condition of the heathen world, and notes that the verb may as well be rendered have not obeyed as have not believed — a character, he says, that belonged to all the heathen nations without exception. Robertson supports the double rendering from the word itself, which means to disbelieve and then to disobey, and translates the clause as a single event in the past: you once upon a time disobeyed God. He also points out how heavily the sentence leans on its adverb, the word now occurring three times in it, so that the whole comparison is between what these readers were and what they presently are.

How the mercy came by way of the other people's unbelief is where Clarke goes further than the rest. He does not let the connection stay merely chronological. What brought the Gentiles in was the method by which God destroyed the Jewish peculiarity and fulfilled the covenant made with Abraham — and that same method is what occasioned the unbelief and the obstinate opposition of the Jews, since it was the removal of their distinctness that they could not bear. On his reading the two halves of the verse name one act of God seen from two sides, and the whole is advanced in favour of the restoration he has been arguing for: a people not so alienated as to be shut out for ever, since the Gentiles addressed here were once as far off and are not.
31:
Where one phrase belongs is unsettled, and Gill flags it before anything else. In the Greek the words about mercy stand attached to the first clause, so that the sense would be that the Jews have not believed in your mercy — which Gill can construe three ways: not believing in Christ, in whom the Gentiles obtained mercy; or not believing the gospel that conveys it; or not believing that mercy belongs to Gentiles at all, having settled into the notion that the Messiah and his blessings are Israel's alone. The English follows Beza, who follows Theophylact, in joining the words to what comes after instead. Robertson takes the same construction and explains its force: the possessive is objective, the mercy shown to you, and it stands early in its clause for emphasis while belonging with the verb that follows. What the sentence then states, he says, is that God's purpose is for the Jews to receive a blessing yet.

On that reading the two peoples serve each other in turn, and Barnes draws out what it commits the church to. The Jews are to be converted by Gentile instrumentality — not by miracle, but in the regular and common way in which God blesses men. It is to be by the Gentiles' mercy, that is, by their taking pity on a condition they are more inclined to despise. And it is to be when great numbers of the Gentiles have themselves been called in. Barnes then turns the exposition into a question about his own day, asking whether the time is not approaching for Gentiles to make the attempt, and admitting frankly that such efforts had so far been unsuccessful; he does not treat that as decisive, holding that the promises will be fulfilled and that Christians will yet be moved with compassion for a people they have written off.

Clarke states the argument as a chain, and the force of it is in the parallel rather than in any new evidence. As surely as the Jews were once in the kingdom and the Gentiles were not; as surely as the Gentiles are now in and the Jews are not; so surely will the Jews be brought back into it. He adds what he thinks will actually change — that they will come in when they consent to acknowledge the Lord Jesus and see it as their privilege to be fellow heirs with the Gentiles of the grace of life. Ellicott keeps to the mechanism already named in the chapter: the sight of the mercy vouchsafed to Gentiles is to act as a stimulus, and so lead to a renewal of Jewish faith and obedience.

Theodoret, who has read the chapter's purpose clauses carefully throughout, will not let this one be pressed. Paul uses the construction in the idiom familiar to him, he says, and the meaning is not that the Jews disbelieved in order that they might find mercy. They disbelieved because of the hardness of their hearts, and will find mercy by turning to a change of mind. He grounds the hope not on any decree but on precedent, reminding the Gentile reader how long all of them lived in sin, and how the merciful Lord did not look at that lengthened ungodliness but blessed whoever was willing to receive his kindness — from which he concludes that nothing would be inconsistent in these being accepted too, whenever they are willing to believe.
32:
The verb is a prison word, and the commentators take it there. Barnes traces its use to men shut up in a jail or a besieged city, and notes it also serves for fish taken in a net, so that all are enclosed by God and released only in his own way and time. Robertson gives the same net image and marks the tense as recording a result already reached by the disbelief of Gentile and Jew alike. Gill rejects a gentler picture — sheaves bound by a band, with unbelief the band — since Paul speaks not of the two together but of each in turn; a prison suits the argument better.

What God's part in this was is the question everyone feels. Gill states it flatly: God is not the author of unbelief or of any other sin, does not put it into men or them into it, but finding them in unbelief concludes them in it and does not yet say to the prisoners, go forth. Barnes works through the same problem in stages. The word does not mean God compelled them to disbelieve, nor that their unbelief was involuntary, since even a justly imprisoned man sinned freely. The keeper who confines a criminal, the judge who condemns him and the officer who executes the sentence do him no wrong, and neither does God — what he does is not to compel men to remain in unbelief but to declare that they are in it, and to hem them about with proof they cannot escape of their need of a Saviour. Calvin's editors gather the same answer from others: Chrysostom paraphrased the verb as God having proved all to be unbelieving, and Pareus answers the how of it in a phrase — by manifesting, accusing and condemning unbelief, but not by effecting or approving it. Theodoret says concluded stands for convicted, and works it differently on each side: the Gentiles convicted by natural judgment and by the creation that taught them, from neither of which they took benefit, and the Jews more heavily still, having the prophets besides.

Clarke turns the whole into a courtroom running into a jail. Both parties had broken God's law, the Jews the written law and the Gentiles the law written in their hearts; both were tried at God's bar, found guilty, condemned to the death they had merited, and locked up under the jailer unbelief awaiting execution — and then a general pardon was proclaimed by the gospel, moved by no merit in either party. The Gentiles welcomed the offer and are out; the Jews refused it on the terms proposed and remain locked up. Since the offers continue without distinction, he expects the day when the Jews, seeing what the Gentile world has come into, will lay hold of the same hope.

What the last clause proves is disputed, and the dispute is short. Calvin makes the emphasis fall on mercy — God is bound to none, and saves freely because all are equally lost — and Barnes quotes him to that effect, adding that it puts every man on a level. Both then close the door on the inference some draw: Calvin calls it extremely gross folly to conclude that all shall be saved, since what is meant is that Jews and Gentiles obtain salvation no otherwise than through mercy, and Robertson makes the same point on the article, that the all are those who receive God's mercy, not that all men are saved. Ellicott takes the sentence furthest, calling it a weighty summary of the whole course of human history and offering it as a motto for the theological side of the theory of evolution — severe as that doctrine may seem, its goal is perfection; and to the objection about the waste of individual life he answers that we see only a part of God's ways.
33:
How many things are being admired is a translation question. The received rendering makes two, tying wisdom and knowledge under riches by the inserted word both; Barnes holds there are three subjects of wonder, and notes that the Syriac and Arabic read so while the English followed the Latin. Ellicott allows either construction and says what survives in both: riches means inexhaustible resources, and by such resources God is able to bring good even out of evil. Calvin's editors report the same division running back to the fathers — Origen, Chrysostom and Theodoret joining riches to depth, Ambrose and Augustine to wisdom — and observe that Paul's usage elsewhere favours the second. Clarke divides the last two words instead: wisdom belongs to the designs, which are therefore right, and knowledge to the means, which are therefore fittest. Henry makes the distinction concretely — knowledge is seeing all that is or was or shall be by one clear and infallible view, wisdom is ordering it to his own purposes.

The metaphor of depth is worked hard. Barnes takes it from the unfathomable sea and applies it to whatever words cannot express. Henry contrasts the shallowness of every other kind of wealth, where one may soon see the bottom, and gives the image the chapter is remembered for: Paul, knowing as much of these mysteries as any man, confesses himself at a loss, and despairing to find the bottom sits down at the brink and adores the depth. Robertson sees the same posture in the syntax: an argument that has carried Paul to the heights and left him on the edge of a precipice, unable to sound the bottom with the plummet of human reason.

The two adjectives at the close are rare, and Robertson identifies them as double compounds, the second borrowed from the language of Job, and draws the distinction they imply: some of God's tracks he has left plain to us and others are beyond us. Henry presses the second image further. God leaves no prints or footsteps behind him and makes no path to shine after him; his ways of providence are new every morning, and he does not go the same way often enough to wear a track. What follows from that, for Henry, is a rule about enquiry — the judgments of God's mouth and the way of our duty are plain and a high road, while the judgments of his hand are dark, and are therefore to be adored rather than pried into.

Calvin turns the exclamation into a discipline. Having spoken from the word and by the Spirit, Paul was at last overcome by the sublimity of the mystery and could do nothing but wonder; so whenever we enter on the eternal counsels of God a bridle should be set on thought and tongue, that after speaking soberly and within the limits of his word our reasoning may end in admiration. There is no shame in this, he adds, unless we claim to be wiser than a man caught up to the third heaven who found no end but to humble himself. Wesley marks the change of scale — in the ninth chapter Paul had sailed in a narrow sea, and now he is in the ocean — and maps the three nouns onto the verses that follow. Cyril presses the smaller case: if the least of God's works are past comprehension, and no one can find a footstep of the Lord, then he who made them all cannot be comprehended either. Theodoret adds that the scheme of the divine economy surpasses human understanding, and that not even the invisible powers reach to the bottom of it; Gill takes the whole outburst as the epilogue of the doctrinal part of the letter, closing everything argued from justification to the restoring of Israel.
34:
The question is borrowed, and Barnes gives its point by contrast. Earthly monarchs keep counsellors of state, to be consulted in perplexity or danger; God sits alone and calls in no creature to advise him, since none is qualified to contribute anything that would enlighten or direct him. The quotation is meant, he adds, to silence opposition and hush complaint, so that a man who cannot trace the reason of God's dealings should still submit. Gill approaches the clause from the side of revelation. The intentions of God's mind could never have been known unless he had disclosed them; even disclosed, they are not known by the natural man, but by the light of the Spirit who makes them known to spiritual men — and even by these not perfectly, but in part, and through a glass darkly.

Calvin sets out two reasons he thinks this verse and the next supply, answering two different complaints. First, all mortals are too blind to take a view of God's predestination by their own understanding, so that reasoning about an unknown thing is presumptuous and absurd. Second, held over for the next verse, no one has any ground of complaint, since nobody can claim God as his debtor. On the wording he prefers the Hebrew idiom of weighing a spirit, which he takes to mean knowing it thoroughly, and observes that if the verb is rendered measure instead, then knowing the mind of the Lord would be taking the measure of his knowledge — which suits the passage.

He then guards the caution against a use he does not want made of it. The warning is not to be applied so as to weaken the certainty of faith, which comes not from the sharpness of the human mind but from the illumination of the Spirit; Paul himself, having said elsewhere that the mysteries of God exceed our comprehension, immediately adds that the faithful do understand the mind of the Lord, having received the Spirit given by God. The distinction Calvin rests on is between God's secret counsel and his will made known in scripture: the whole doctrine of scripture rises above the human mind, yet access to it is not closed to those who follow the Spirit soberly, while the hidden counsel has a depth no investigation reaches. Where the Spirit leaves us, he says, there we should stop and fix our standing, since anyone seeking to know more than God has revealed will be overwhelmed by the brightness of an inaccessible light.

Clarke reads the verse as a rebuke to a particular kind of writing, and names an instance. It is strange, he says, that with such a text before them men should sit down and write coolly about counsels and decrees formed from all eternity, speaking with as much confidence as if they had sat in the council of the Most High. The example he gives is a writer who drew out a scheme of absolute reprobation with all its causes and effects, and a matching scheme of election, link by link in graduated order — and closed the whole with this very exclamation about ways past finding out. The man forgot, Clarke observes, that he had just searched out the judgments in the one case and found out the ways in the other, and had offered the finished diagram as proof of his success. Clarke concludes that since we cannot comprehend God we cannot comprehend his operations, and that the objects of his mercy should adore in silence and obey with alacrity. Robertson, from another quarter, ends on the same note in a line: some men seem to feel competent for the job. Ellicott adds the structural observation that the two clauses here answer to the wisdom and the knowledge, as the next verse answers to the riches.
35:
The third question completes a pattern, and Theodoret is the one who lays the pattern out. The three interrogatives answer to the three nouns of the doxology in reverse: who hath known the mind of the Lord to the knowledge, who hath been his counsellor to the wisdom, and this one about giving first to the riches. He then says what those riches are — so immense the riches of his goodness that he gave existence to what was not, and to what exists gave well-being of his free grace — and adds the tenderness he finds in the arrangement: nothing is really due to us for anything we first gave, and yet in mercy God condescends to call each free gift a repayment. Ellicott states the same connection more briefly, that the means by which God works are not supplied to him from without but proceed from his own boundless stores.

The quotation comes from Job, and its wording is discussed. Barnes points to the challenge there — who has prevented me, that I should repay him? — and explains that the older English word means to anticipate or go before, so that the question is who has conferred a favour on God first and thereby laid him under obligation. He notes that the same passage adds that whatever is under the whole heaven is God's, and observes that Paul is using it against the prevailing doctrine of his countrymen: nobody can plead merit or advance a claim, so every favour of salvation must be conferred by grace, and God may bestow it when and where he pleases. Robertson marks the verb as occurring nowhere else in the New Testament and notes that Paul's rendering is his own and not the Greek version's, and that the verb for repaying is one Paul uses elsewhere in a bad sense as well as this good one.

Calvin makes the verse a defence of God's righteousness against a specific accusation. Unrighteousness could only be charged if God failed to render each his due, but no one is deprived of a right, since he is under obligation to none; a man who would constrain another to do him good must produce the deeds that earned it, and no one can. He then pushes the point past the obvious case. It is not only our corrupt and sinful nature that leaves us with nothing to bring — Calvin denies that even a perfect man could produce anything by which he might gain God's favour, since from the first moment of his existence he is already so indebted by the right of creation that he has nothing of his own. Gill runs the same argument down the scale of creatures: Adam in innocence could give God nothing, nor can the angels in heaven, much less sinful men on earth, whose bodies and souls and every enjoyment and everything good in them came from him in the first place; from which he concludes that no one can merit anything at God's hands.

Clarke asks the questions rather than answering them, and aims them at the quarrel the chapter has been settling. Who can pretend to have any demands on God, and to whom is he indebted? Have Jews or Gentiles any right to his blessings? Does he do the Jews an injustice in choosing the Gentiles, and was it because he owed the Gentiles something that he chose them? He offers the standing challenge in the text — let anyone with a claim prefer it, and he shall be compensated — and then closes it with three questions of another kind, how the Creator can be indebted to the creature, how the cause can depend on the effect, and how the Father of every good gift can be under obligation to those he provides for and who depend wholly on his bounty.
36:
Three prepositions carry the whole sentence, and every witness assigns them the same three roles. Robertson names them Source, Agent and Goal, and reports Alford's verdict on the passage they close: the sublimest apostrophe in the pages of inspiration. Barnes takes the first to mean that God is the original fountain of all blessings, the second that he not merely planned but acts, creating and directing by his own power, and the third to name the end for which everything was made. That end is not God's happiness, since he was eternally happy, nor any addition to him, since he is infinite, but that he might act as God and receive what is due to God. Wesley compresses them into Creator, Preserver and ultimate end, and reads the closing word as where the apostle's affection, risen to its height, shuts everything up. Gill applies them to grace as well as nature, so that election, redemption and regeneration alike spring from God's will, are brought about by his power, and issue in his glory.

Calvin treats the verse as proof of the one before it. We cannot glory in anything of our own against God, having been created by him out of nothing and existing through him now; our being should therefore be spent on making his glory known, since it would be strange in creatures whom he formed and sustains to live for any other purpose. He states the alternative as an absurdity: the order of nature would be subverted if God, the beginning of all things, were not also the end. Barnes closes the letter's argument with observations drawn from the verse. He who formed all things has a right to all, and he on whom all depend has a right to homage. It becomes a man to be humble, since he sees few of the reasons of an infinite God's doings and cannot sit in judgment on them — though nothing, Barnes adds, is more common than men reasoning about the divine mind as if fit to counsel infinite wisdom. And the universe made by him is fitted to declare his glory, the government of free minds a greater wonder still than the rolling of the planets.

Whether the prepositions carry more than they say is the one real disagreement. Ellicott calls it a mistake to find an allusion to the Trinity here, as some older commentators did: the subject appears to be God the Father, and the prominent idea the unity of creation answering to the unity of the Godhead — though in more analytical passages this very use of the prepositions would express the threefold relation of origination, mediate causation and return. Theodoret uses the verse in the opposite direction and against a named party. Paul, he says, recognised no difference between of whom and through whom, as though the first marked a superiority proper to the Father and the second an inferiority suited to the Son, since he applies both to one Person; so if the Arians and Eunomians take the subject to be the Father they will find through whom joined to it, and if they refer it to the Son they will find of whom joined instead.

Clarke notices the formula was not unique to Paul, quoting the emperor Marcus Antoninus addressing Nature as God — of thee are all things, in thee are all things, to thee are all things — and suggesting he had borrowed it from this epistle. His closing observation is about the asymmetry of what can be explained. God's dispensations never contradict reason, though they surpass it, and we can far more easily account for his justice than for his mercy: ten thousand reasons appear why he should display the one, and scarcely a reason for the other — and yet the displays for which no reason can be found are the greater and the more numerous.
